strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: learning useful robot-centric visual representations without segmentation masks or CAD-based supervision. Conditioning future-frame prediction on proprioception is intuitive and potentially useful.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with an understandable architecture, explicit objectives, and substantial hyperparameter and compute information.

The evaluation includes a real-world interaction dataset and ten simulated manipulation tasks, with comparisons to DrQ-v2 and the closely related supervised SEAR method. The reported average gains are promising.

The prediction-horizon and loss-weight studies provide some useful sensitivity evidence, and the authors candidly acknowledge limitations such as motor babbling, few seeds, and restricted experimental scope.
weaknesses: The central disentanglement claim is not convincingly established. The objective does not identify or enforce an agent/environment factorization: the scene latent can retain agent information, while the proprioceptive branch can encode correlated object motion. BAIR evidence consists only of a few qualitative examples, with no mask-based localization, representation probing, reconstruction metrics, quantitative held-out-trajectory evaluation, or comparison to video-prediction baselines. The single handcrafted trajectory has no ground truth and cannot demonstrate generalization.

The claimed action-regularization mechanism is unsupported. The auxiliary loss is attached to critic/shared-representation training and does not explicitly penalize actor actions or their unpredictability. No measurement shows that learned actions become more predictable, and improved returns could simply result from auxiliary representation learning.

Essential controls are missing. There is no matched baseline using the same architecture and future-prediction loss without the proposed factorization, no ablation of the similarity term or proprioceptive conditioning, and the beta study omits beta=0. Most importantly, Ego-Foresight alone receives 50,000 steps of structured motor babbling; applying the identical exploration schedule to DrQ-v2 and SEAR is necessary to rule out exploration as the source of the gains.

The RL evidence is statistically weak. Results use only three seeds and highly variable min-max bands, without confidence intervals or significance tests. Table 1 reports the maximum mean success over training checkpoints rather than performance at a fixed budget or an area-under-curve measure, creating selection bias. The 23% efficiency calculation also substitutes the final horizon for methods that never reach the threshold, making the aggregation difficult to interpret.

Several implementation details needed to assess soundness are ambiguous. In particular, the paper defines the proprioceptive representation using future sequences but does not clearly specify its causal construction at policy-execution time, how features are supplied to actor and critic, or which gradients update each encoder. Enforcing a scene representation to be constant within an episode may also suppress task-relevant object-state changes, but this issue is neither analyzed nor ablated.

Generality is limited to one robot morphology appearing in both datasets, selected Meta-World tasks, and one RL algorithm. There is no real-robot control experiment, alternative embodiment, camera/domain shift, or substantive tool/body-schema adaptation study. Code is only promised for future release, further limiting current verification.

The headline 23% efficiency number uses a nonstandard threshold and substitutes the final training budget when a method never reaches that threshold, making the aggregate sensitive to censoring and arbitrary task budgets; neither headline aggregate has uncertainty.

The ablations are too narrow to support causal claims. The beta study covers one task and omits beta=0; the horizon study covers another task without uncertainty; alpha, motor babbling, proprioception, architecture/capacity, and individual loss terms are not ablated. Moreover, the plotted horizon results do not clearly substantiate the assertion that performance stabilizes beyond H=10.

Generality is limited: both the real-video data and simulator use a Sawyer robot, policy learning is evaluated only in simulation, and only one RL algorithm and camera/setup are considered. The real-world results do not demonstrate real-world control or sample-efficiency.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the checklist claim: the supplied manuscript contains no accessible code link or algorithmic pseudocode, and omits important details such as exact Meta-World/software versions, policy-time feature construction, plot smoothing, and the precise aggregation used for the 8% and 23% claims.

Overall, this is a promising but incremental combination of established conditioned prediction, slow-feature similarity, and auxiliary-loss RL. Given the confounded comparison and unsupported central mechanism and disentanglement claims, the current evidence is not competitive at a top-tier AI venue.

Ego-Foresight is conceptually simple and can be integrated into replay-buffer-based visual RL as an auxiliary action-conditioned prediction objective.

The evaluation has useful breadth: 25 simulated tasks, five seeds, and comparisons with DrQ-v2, the supervised SEAR baseline, and Dreamer-v3. The reported gains on several Meta-World tasks are potentially interesting.
The qualitative predictions suggest that the model captures controllable motion, including motion of a held tool, and the paper is reasonably clear about its failure under visual distractions.
weaknesses: The central claim of agent–environment disentanglement is not established. The objective has no constraint preventing agent information from leaking into the scene features or arbitrary action-correlated objects from entering the agent features. Gradient visualizations and a few reconstructions are not quantitative evidence of disentanglement.

The RL improvements cannot be attributed specifically to agent awareness. Ego-Foresight changes the architecture and capacity, adds a reconstruction/forward-prediction loss, and introduces a 25k-step extreme-action babbling phase. There are no matched controls such as DrQ-v2 with identical babbling and capacity, full-scene prediction, reconstruction without the split, or a split representation without prediction.

The tool and embodiment-adaptation claims are substantially overstated. A hammer moving predictably within a trained task does not demonstrate adaptation to a changed body schema. There is no evaluation on unseen tools or morphologies, no measurement of adaptation speed, and no comparison against supervised approaches under such changes.

The real-world and trajectory-generalization evidence is only qualitative. BAIR is an offline dataset rather than a physical control experiment, and the unseen-trajectory claim rests on one handcrafted example without quantitative held-out evaluation or baselines.

Results are mixed: the method underperforms DrQ-v2 on the aggregate Distracting DMC result and trails Dreamer-v3 or SEAR on many DMC and Meta-World tasks. The broad claims of improved performance and competitiveness with model-based methods are therefore stronger than the evidence.

The statistical analysis is inadequate for noisy RL experiments. Five-seed means and standard deviations are shown without confidence intervals, significance tests, robust aggregate statistics, or per-task numerical tables. The custom threshold-based aggregate score is underspecified and has no uncertainty estimate.

The ablation study is confined to one Meta-World task and mostly sweeps hyperparameters. It does not isolate the essential structural choices or show that conclusions generalize across tasks and visual conditions.

Novelty relative to action-conditioned video prediction, content–motion factorization, and self-predictive auxiliary objectives is limited. Stronger comparisons with these closely related alternatives are needed.

Reproducibility is poor: there is no usable code or appendix, and important architecture, optimization, task-selection, preprocessing, baseline-configuration, and aggregate-normalization details are missing. The acknowledged computational overhead is also not quantified.
The proposed ±1 motor-babbling procedure may be unsafe or impractical on physical robots, which conflicts with the real-world motivation and is not addressed.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and appealing idea: learning agent-aware representations without simulator-provided masks by combining an action-conditioned predictive bottleneck with a bypassed scene representation.

The empirical scope is substantial, covering 25 manipulation and locomotion tasks across Meta-World, Distracting DMC, and Hurdle DMC, with five seeds and comparisons against the underlying DrQ-v2 algorithm, the supervised SEAR method, and Dreamer-v3.
Results on Meta-World are encouraging: Ego-Foresight improves over DrQ-v2 on many tasks and shows particularly strong aggregate performance on the selected tool-related tasks.
The inclusion of real-robot BAIR data, qualitative tool-motion examples, and ablations over loss weight, horizon, feature dimension, and motor-babbling duration provides useful breadth.
The paper is generally well motivated and clearly written, and it candidly identifies the degradation under visual distractions and the computational overhead as limitations.
weaknesses: The central claim of agent-environment disentanglement is not established quantitatively. Gradient visualizations and a few reconstructions do not show that agent information is confined to the agent features or excluded from the scene features. Mask-based localization metrics, latent probes, feature swapping, or intervention tests would provide much stronger evidence.

The source of the RL improvement is substantially confounded. Ego-Foresight adds model capacity, a reconstruction/prediction objective, and a 25,000-step motor-babbling phase. The paper lacks controls such as DrQ-v2 with identical babbling, a parameter-matched auxiliary predictor without the proposed split, and reconstruction without action-conditioned agent prediction. This is especially important because the babbling ablation indicates that exploration itself contributes materially.

The claimed body-schema and tool adaptation is demonstrated only through qualitative, in-distribution sequences such as the hammer example. There is no held-out-tool experiment, morphology change, adaptation-speed measurement, or quantitative comparison showing an advantage over supervised representations.

The real-world evidence is limited to a few qualitative BAIR examples and one handcrafted trajectory. Dataset splits, quantitative prediction or localization metrics, comparisons, and downstream real-robot control experiments are absent, so the real-world and unseen-trajectory claims are stronger than the evidence.

Generalization across benchmarks is mixed: the method underperforms plain DrQ-v2 on the Distracting DMC aggregate and is substantially below Dreamer-v3 on several DMC tasks. Thus, the broad claim of competitiveness with model-based methods needs qualification.

Evaluation and reporting have notable gaps. Ablations use only one Meta-World task, aggregate scores lack uncertainty or significance analysis, the custom snapshot metric is insufficiently validated, and Figure 1 reports two Hurdle DMC tasks while Figure 7 appears to show three, creating an unexplained inconsistency with the stated total of 25 tasks.

Reproducibility is limited by missing architectural layer specifications, optimization and update details, task-selection rationale, exact numerical result tables, and quantitative wall-clock or compute costs. No usable code or supplementary-material pointer is evident in the manuscript.

The simulated evaluation is reasonably broad, covering 25 tasks across Meta-World, Distracting DMC, and Hurdle DMC with five seeds and relevant baselines including supervised SEAR and Dreamer-v3.
Ego-Foresight produces meaningful gains on Meta-World, particularly on the designated tool tasks, where its reported aggregate score substantially exceeds those of the compared methods.
The paper includes several hyperparameter ablations, qualitative BAIR results, and a candid discussion of failures under visual distractions and of computational overhead.
weaknesses: The central claim of learning a disentangled or agent-aware representation is not convincingly established. Gradient visualizations and selected reconstructions are qualitative proxies; there are no segmentation probes, leakage measurements, quantitative disentanglement metrics, or controlled tests showing that agent information resides specifically in the proposed subspace. The objective also permits agent information in the scene features and any action-correlated environmental motion in the agent features.

Crucial causal controls are missing: capacity-matched DrQ-v2, DrQ-v2 with the same 25,000-step motor-babbling schedule, generic reconstruction or full-frame action-conditioned prediction, a no-split representation, and shuffled-action controls. Consequently, the gains cannot be attributed to agent-awareness rather than additional parameters, auxiliary predictive regularization, or altered exploration. The single-task beta and babbling ablations do not resolve this issue.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently documented. Ego-Foresight changes the encoder, adds a recurrent model and decoder, and changes early data collection, while baselines apparently use their defaults. Parameter counts, compute budgets, wall-clock costs, and matched exploration schedules are not reported.

The empirical picture is mixed and the claims are overstated. Ego-Foresight underperforms plain DrQ-v2 on the Distracting DMC aggregate and substantially trails Dreamer-v3 on both DMC aggregates. No statistical tests or aggregate uncertainty support the claimed 17-of-25 improvement count or the assertion that it often outperforms model-based methods.

The real-world and embodiment-adaptation evidence is too weak. BAIR is used only for selected qualitative offline predictions, without quantitative metrics or video-prediction baselines. One handcrafted trajectory does not establish out-of-distribution imagination, and the hammer example does not demonstrate adaptation speed, held-out-tool generalization, or real-world control. The claim that such adaptation is impossible for supervised methods is also too strong.

Evaluation reporting is incomplete: the custom aggregate score depends on observed maxima and selected thresholds but its normalization is unclear, numerical tables and confidence intervals are absent, and Figure 1 labels Hurdle DMC as two tasks while Figure 7 shows three. These issues make the summary comparisons difficult to verify.

Reproducibility is below top-tier expectations: important architecture, optimization, preprocessing, evaluation, task-selection, and baseline-tuning details are omitted; there is no algorithmic pseudocode, full configuration, or code-release information. Overall, the idea and Meta-World results are promising, but the missing controls and unsupported central interpretation are major rather than marginal deficiencies.

strengths: The action-conditioned bottleneck is intuitive and removes the simulator-derived agent masks required by the closest supervised baseline.
The RL evaluation is broad: 25 manipulation and locomotion tasks, three benchmark families, five seeds, per-task curves, and comparisons with DrQ-v2, SEAR, and Dreamer-v3.
Ego-Foresight improves DrQ-v2 on 17 of 25 tasks and shows particularly promising aggregate results on Meta-World tool tasks.
The paper examines varied embodiments, visual distractors, real robot video, and several method-specific hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central agent-environment disentanglement claim is not quantitatively established. Gradient visualizations and selected reconstructions do not show that the agent features exclusively encode the agent or that scene features exclude it; simulator masks could support direct localization or probing evaluations.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed mechanism from generic auxiliary prediction, extra model capacity, the encoder projection, or the 25k-step motor-babbling schedule. The matched beta=0 ablation covers only one task, and there is no action-conditioned full-frame or latent-forward-prediction baseline.

Claims about embodiment adaptation and real-world generalization rely on a few qualitative examples. The handcrafted trajectory has no executed ground truth, quantitative prediction metric, or competing video-prediction baseline, and no real-world policy learning is evaluated.

Results are mixed: the method does not improve DrQ-v2 on Distracting DMC and trails SEAR and Dreamer-v3 on aggregate Hurdle DMC. Uncertainty for aggregate scores and statistical comparisons are absent.
The custom threshold-based aggregate metric is insufficiently justified, and Figure 1 reports two Hurdle tasks while the per-task figure appears to contain three, leaving the aggregation unclear.

Claims of compatibility with arbitrary model-free or model-based algorithms are unsupported by the single DrQ-v2 integration. Reproducibility is also limited by missing implementation-level architecture, optimization, data-split, compute, and wall-clock details.
